Leummim
leh-UM-mim
n. pl. (a people descended from Dedan, son of Jokshan, by Keturah)
Hebrew Le'ummim, peoples, or nations, from le'om, a people; named once, Genesis 25:3.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · In the Text · Related

Biblical Definition

The Leummim are the last of the three peoples sprung from Dedan in the line of Abraham by Keturah: “And Jokshan begat Sheba, and Dedan. And the sons of Dedan were Asshurim, and Letushim, and Leummim” (Genesis 25:3). The line begins in the verse that opens the chapter: “Then again Abraham took a wife, and her name was Keturah” (Genesis 25:1). These are Abraham's children too, and the register of them is one of the quiet proofs of the promise that he should be a father of many nations. The name means simply peoples. They are not heard of again, and they have no part in the covenant line, which the next verses settle plainly: Abraham gave gifts to the sons of the concubines and sent them away eastward, and “Abraham gave all that he had unto Isaac” (Genesis 25:5). The sorting is deliberate and it is the pattern of election. Many came out of Abraham; one line carried the promise. Paul builds the argument of Romans 9 on exactly this: they are not all children of Abraham that are of his seed, for in Isaac shall thy seed be called.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): Leummim, peoples; a people descended from Dedan, grandson of Abraham by Keturah, named once, Genesis 25:3.

Hebrew Le'ummim, peoples, or nations.

From le'om, a people or a tribe.

It occurs once in the Authorized Version, Genesis 25:3.

Descended from Dedan, son of Jokshan, son of Abraham by Keturah.

They have no part in the covenant line, which ran through Isaac.

Key Scripture

Gen 25:3 — "And Jokshan begat Sheba, and Dedan. And the sons of Dedan were Asshurim, and Letushim, and Leummim."

Gen 25:1 — "Then again Abraham took a wife, and her name was Keturah."

Gen 25:5 — "And Abraham gave all that he had unto Isaac."

Rom 9:7 — "Neither, because they are the seed of Abraham, are they all children: but, In Isaac shall thy seed be called."

Modern Corruption

Election is softened into God's general goodwill toward all; Genesis 25 shows Abraham's many sons sent away with gifts and the promise given to one.

expand to see more

The doctrine of election is nowhere more plainly illustrated than in the household of Abraham, and nowhere more consistently avoided. Abraham fathered Ishmael, then Isaac, then six sons by Keturah with peoples descending from them — Leummim among those grandchildren. All were his seed. One line received the covenant. Scripture states the division without apology: the sons of the concubines received gifts and were sent eastward, and Abraham gave all that he had unto Isaac.

Paul takes up this very history to answer the objection that God's word had failed: neither, because they are the seed of Abraham, are they all children; but, In Isaac shall thy seed be called. Unconditional election is therefore not a late Reformed imposition on the text but the argument the apostle draws out of Genesis. The Leummim are a nation that came of Abraham and never heard the promise, and their existence in the register is part of how Scripture teaches that the promise is God's to place.
